discovery: Optical detection and coherent control of single electron spins in diamond, and their development into nanoscale quantum sensors
subfield: Quantum science and technology / solid-state spin physics
motivation: Wrachtrup made the first optical detection of magnetic resonance from a single nitrogen-vacancy (NV) defect spin in diamond and then demonstrated its coherent control at room temperature. This turned an isolated solid-state spin into a quantum system that can be read out, controlled and engineered. Lukin and Walsworth, working together and in parallel with Wrachtrup, showed that this single spin works as an atomic-scale magnetometer. Their 2008 experiments reached nanoscale resolution and sensitivity, and the three groups later extended the method to nuclear magnetic resonance on nanoliter-to-zeptoliter samples, imaging of magnetic fields in living cells, condensed-matter imaging and spin-photon interfaces. Their work founded the field of solid-state quantum sensing, which hundreds of laboratories and a growing industry now use in physics, geoscience, biology and materials research. It also showed that defect spins in wide-bandgap materials could serve as practical qubits, and that idea has since driven work on quantum networks.
